newsitem.title: JAPAN: NORDIC SKIING-OGIWARA DISMISSES CONCERN ABOUT AGE.
newsitem.headline: NORDIC SKIING-OGIWARA DISMISSES CONCERN ABOUT AGE.

text.p: Kenji Ogiwara, brushing aside concerns about both age and indifferent form, is preparing quietly for a final Olympics in his home town of Nagono next year.
Ogiwara captured gold in the Nordic skiing team event at the 1992 Albertville Olympics and went on to win an unprecedented three consecutive World Cup individual overall titles from 1993-1995.
He also helped keep Japan at the top of the team event when they won the world championships in 1993 and 1995 and captured the gold medal at the 1994 Olympics.
The former "King of Skiing" finished sixth in the World Cup overall standings, sparking speculation that at 27 his career might be over.
But Ogiwara showed that he was still a force to be reckoned with by winning the individual gold at the world championships in Norway last February.
"I was able to perform well at a major event like the world championships. That gave me confidence ahead of the Nagano games," the Japanese skier said.
Ogiwara said he also has a "home court" advantage at Nagano, adding he was able to perform well at a World Cup event held in early February at Hakuba, the site of Nordic events at the 1998 Games.

"It's my home ground. I'm used to jumping on the hill at Hakuba. Mentally as well, everything is familiar -- the scenary, the food, and the hill. I was able to relax and get a good feeling (at the Hakuba World Cup). So I think there is a 'homecourt' advantage," he said.
Ogiwara finished fifth in the Hakuba World Cup, but had been in second place after the jumping event. The combined event consists of a jumping event, followed by a cross-country race.
The former World Cup overall titleholder also dismissed claims that he was already past his best.

"Age does not matter. The one who wins is the best," Ogiwara said, adding that his experience gave him an edge over younger skiers. "Young guys still get nervous and crush under pressure. In that sense I have an advantage."
Ogiwara was brought up in Kusatsu, a town about 200 kms northwest of Tokyo. Kusatsu is a popular winter resort with spas and a skiing resort.
"Alpine skiing was something that we did for fun, because I was brought up in Kusatsu. But I wanted to do something different, like jumping. To me, alpine was just making turns," Ogiwara said.
Ogiwara's twin brother Tsugiharu, who also competes in the World Cup, had generally performed better until entering college.
"When Tsugiharu first made it to the national games in junior high school, and I had to stay at home, I cried," Ogiwara said.
His competitive fires have not dimimished.
"Those who have not won a gold at the Olympics would say the World Cup is the pinnacle, and those who have won the gold would say the Olympics is the one," he said.
"So the best thing to do is to win them all."
